claims.text: We chose pgvector because vector search then runs inside the same PostgreSQL instance as authorization and revisions, so the team keeps one store, one backup and one transaction boundary instead of a second service to operate.
The claim index keeps one row per current claim of the current memory revision.
Migration 0003_memory_brain fixes the embedding dimension at 1536, so a new model needs a new migration.
Cosine distance ranks claims, and the model transport normalizes every vector before we write it.
We rejected a separate vector service because it adds a second store and a second authorization path.
The development database runs PostgreSQL 17.6 with pgvector 0.8.2 installed in the space schema.
The production database runs PostgreSQL 17.6 with pgvector 0.7.4, and the managed upgrade window opens in October, so we refuse an untested version bump on the store that holds every claim index row.
A GIN index over the cue hash array serves cue expansion, and an HNSW index serves nearest-neighbour search.
Naming a migration badly cost us an hour of confusion during the review, so revision identifiers stay descriptive.
Open question: does pgvector 0.8 iterative scan behave correctly under our row-level security predicate?

Claim text never enters the index table. It stays inside the encrypted revision under the same AES-GCM key scope as other content, so a database export reveals similarity and equality but never the wording of a claim.
The API runs FastAPI on Python 3.13, and the website is Next.js running on Cloudflare Workers.
Decision: PostgreSQL stays the only authoritative store, so there is no second database for vectors.
